cards.front: What six basic factors comprise the modern ACSM FITT-VP framework for exercise prescription?
cards.back:
The six core factors of the FITT-VP framework are:
  • F - Frequency: How often exercise is performed per week.
  • I - Intensity: The level of exertion or physiological strain during the exercise bout.
  • T - Type (Mode): The specific exercise modality performed.
  • T - Time (Duration): The length of time spent in an exercise session.
  • V - Volume: The cumulative total amount of exercise performed per week.
  • P - Progression: The systematic advancement of the exercise workload over time.

cards.front: What is the minimal training threshold concept in aerobic exercise prescription, and how does it vary among individuals?
cards.back:
A specific minimal threshold for frequency, duration, and intensity must be exceeded to elicit cardiorespiratory endurance adaptations. This threshold varies based on baseline fitness level:
  • Healthy Adults: The lower moderate intensity threshold is defined as 40% of Heart Rate Reserve (HRR) or 40% of VO2max.
  • Low-Fit / Deconditioned Individuals: Aerobic fitness improvements can occur at exercise intensities below 40% VO2max.
  • Progression: As cardiorespiratory endurance improves, an individual's minimal training threshold progressively increases.

cards.front: What are the optimal weekly exercise frequency recommendations for moderate versus vigorous physical activity?
cards.back:
Optimal health-related cardiorespiratory benefits are achieved with a time investment of 3 to 5 days per week:
  • Moderate-Intensity Activity: Optimal frequency is 5 days per week.
  • Vigorous-Intensity Activity: Optimal frequency is 3 days per week.
Note: Participating 6 to 7 days per week provides additional caloric expenditure for weight loss, but high daily frequency should not be encouraged until exercise habits are established to minimize musculoskeletal injury risk.

cards.front: How does the ACSM categorize moderate versus vigorous exercise intensity, and why is intensity the most critical factor?
cards.back:
Exercise intensity is the single most critical factor for developing cardiorespiratory endurance. ACSM defines exercise intensity zones as:
  • Moderate Intensity: 40% to 59% of Heart Rate Reserve (HRR) or VO2max.
  • Vigorous Intensity: 60% to 90% of Heart Rate Reserve (HRR) or VO2max.

cards.front: What physiological adaptations result from High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT), and how does its time efficiency compare to continuous endurance training?
cards.back: Low-volume, very high-intensity HIIT produces cardiorespiratory and metabolic adaptations similar to high-volume, lower-intensity continuous endurance training. Substantial increases in skeletal muscle oxidative capacity, cardiometabolic health markers, and aerobic endurance performance can be achieved in interventions as brief as 10 minutes per day over 2 weeks.

cards.front: How are exercise duration and intensity related, and how do single continuous sessions compare to accumulated shorter bouts?
cards.back:
Duration and intensity are inversely related. Key principles include:
  • Optimal Session Duration: Sustaining an appropriate intensity for 20 to 30 minutes per day provides optimal cardiovascular conditioning for time invested.
  • Bout Accumulation: Similar cardiorespiratory improvements occur whether daily endurance training is performed in a single continuous session (e.g., 1 x 30 min) or accumulated in multiple shorter bouts (e.g., 3 x 10 min bouts lasting ≥ 10 min each).
  • Weight Loss: Longer continuous bouts are primarily prescribed to maximize total caloric expenditure.

cards.front: How is weekly exercise volume calculated using MET-minutes, and what are the ACSM target volume guidelines?
cards.back:
Exercise volume combines intensity, frequency, and duration into a single quantifiable metric:
  • MET-Minutes Calculation: Activity intensity in METs x total weekly minutes (where 1 MET = resting oxygen uptake of ~3.5 mL O2/kg/min).
  • ACSM Target Volume: Recommended weekly volume is ≥ 500 to 1,000 MET-minutes/week, which equals approximately 150 minutes/week of moderate-intensity exercise.
  • Caloric Equivalent: Corresponds to 1,000 to 1,500 kcal/week expended in physical activity.

cards.front: How should exercise progression be managed according to principles of training overload?
cards.back: Progression involves systematically advancing one or more FITT-VP components over time to maintain progressive overload as fitness improves. Progression must be individualized based on age, initial fitness level, and health goals, and should be advanced gradually (typically increasing duration before intensity) to prevent musculoskeletal injury or excessive physiological fatigue.

cards.front: How is sedentary behavior defined physiologically, and what acute pathophysiological changes occur after 30 minutes of continuous sitting?
cards.back:
Sedentary behavior is defined as any waking activity requiring an energy expenditure of < 1.5 METs while sitting, reclining, or lying down (comprising ~60% of waking hours). As few as 30 minutes of continuous sitting induces acute pathophysiological changes:
  • Insulin Resistance: Rapid elevation in acute insulin resistance.
  • Impaired Lipid/Carbohydrate Metabolism: Suppressed lipoprotein lipase (LPL) activity and metabolic shift prioritizing glucose utilization and fat storage.
  • Subacute Inflammation: Promotion of systemic, subacute vascular inflammation and changes in muscle fiber characteristics.

cards.front: Why does regular structured exercise not counteract sedentary sitting, and what movement threshold effectively breaks sedentary physiology?
cards.back:
Key clinical distinctions between exercise and sedentary behavior include:
  • Exercise Limitation: Regular structured exercise (e.g., 30-60 min/day) improves VO2max but does NOT reverse or counteract the negative cardiometabolic effects of continuous, prolonged sitting during the rest of the day.
  • Movement Break Threshold: Engaging in as little as 2 minutes of low-intensity physical activity (2.0 to 2.5 METs) periodically during prolonged sitting directly interrupts sedentary physiology, restoring normal glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity.
